content.summary: Everything in the universe is made of tiny particles called atoms. Atoms themselves are made of three even smaller particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons.
content.tip: Atomic Number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons (in a neutral atom). Mass Number (A) = protons + neutrons.
content.memory: ⚠️ Electrons are SO light (1/1840 of a proton) that we often ignore their mass when calculating mass number!
content.analogy: Think of an atom like a tiny solar system: the nucleus is the Sun (tiny but heavy), electrons are planets orbiting around it.

quiz.question: How many neutrons are in a ₁₇³⁵Cl atom?
quiz.explanation: For ₁₇³⁵Cl: neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18. The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

content.summary: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) but with different numbers of neutrons — so they have different mass numbers.
content.formula: Aᵣ = Σ(mass × relative abundance) / Σ(relative abundances)
content.formula_example: Example: Cl has ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%) → Aᵣ = (35×75 + 37×25) / 100 = 35.5
content.tip: The 'r' in Aᵣ stands for 'relative'. Aᵣ has NO units — it's just a ratio compared to carbon-12.
content.memory: Isotopes = same Z, different A. They behave the same chemically (same electrons) but have different masses!

quiz.question: Bromine has two isotopes: ⁷⁹Br (50%) and ⁸¹Br (50%). What is the relative atomic mass?
quiz.hint: Apply the formula: Aᵣ = (mass₁ × abundance₁ + mass₂ × abundance₂) / total abundance
quiz.explanation: Aᵣ = (79 × 50 + 81 × 50) / 100 = (3950 + 4050) / 100 = 80. Notice that 50%+50%=100%, so it's simply the average of 79 and 81.

content.summary: A mass spectrometer is a powerful tool that measures the mass and abundance of isotopes with incredible precision. It can find exact isotopic masses and calculate Aᵣ.

steps.name: Vaporisation
steps.desc: Sample is turned into a gas

steps.name: Ionisation
steps.desc: High-energy electrons knock off one electron → M⁺ ions

steps.name: Acceleration
steps.desc: Electric field speeds up all ions to the same kinetic energy

steps.name: Deflection
steps.desc: Magnetic field bends ion paths — lighter ions (low m/z) deflect MORE

steps.name: Detection
steps.desc: Ions arrive at detector, creating peaks on the mass spectrum

content.tip: Acceleration uses an ELECTRIC field. Deflection uses a MAGNETIC field. Different forces, different jobs!
content.memory: The mass spectrum shows: x-axis = m/z (mass/charge ratio), y-axis = relative abundance (%). Each peak is one isotope.
content.formula: m/z = mass / charge. Since most ions are singly charged (+1), m/z ≈ mass number.

quiz.question: In a mass spectrometer, which field is used to deflect ions?
options: C. Both electric and magnetic fields
quiz.explanation: The ELECTRIC field accelerates ions (Step 3). The MAGNETIC field deflects them (Step 4). These are two separate, sequential processes. Step 4 deflection separates ions by their m/z ratio.

content.summary: Electrons don't orbit the nucleus like planets! Instead, they occupy regions called orbitals — where each orbital can hold a maximum of 2 electrons.
content.fill_note: ⚠️ 4s fills BEFORE 3d (lower energy). But 3d is emptied before 4s in transition metals!
content.hunds_rule: When filling orbitals of the same energy (like the 3 p orbitals), electrons go into EMPTY orbitals FIRST, with parallel spins.
content.example: Nitrogen (Z=7): 1s² 2s² 2p³. The 3 p electrons each go into a separate p orbital (Hund's Rule).
content.tip: The filling order follows the diagonal rule — trace diagonals from top-right to bottom-left on your subshell energy diagram.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the correct electron configuration for nitrogen (Z=7)?
quiz.hint: Count electrons: Z=7 means 7 electrons total. Fill in order: 1s (2), then 2s (2), remaining electrons go to 2p.
quiz.explanation: Filling: 1s² (2 e⁻) + 2s² (2 e⁻) + 2p³ (3 e⁻) = 7 electrons total. The notation shows how many electrons are in each subshell.

content.summary: First ionisation energy (IE₁) is the energy needed to remove one electron from one mole of gaseous atoms.
content.trend_period: Across a period (left → right): IE generally INCREASES because nuclear charge increases, pulling electrons closer.
content.trend_group: Down a group: IE DECREASES because inner electron shells increase (more shielding), and outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.

exceptions.reason: Electron enters a new p subshell (2p vs 2s) — higher energy, easier to remove
Electron pairing in a p orbital causes repulsion — one electron is easier to remove

content.successive_ie: Each successive IE is larger than the previous. A BIG JUMP indicates all electrons in one shell have been removed — revealing how many outer electrons the atom has.
content.tip: The position of the big jump tells you the GROUP number! If IE₂→IE₃ is the big jump, the atom has 2 outer electrons = Group 2.
content.example: Na has tiny IE₁, then a MASSIVE jump to IE₂. This proves Na has 1 outer electron (Group 1).

quiz.question: Successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): 590, 1145, 4912, 6474... Which group is this element in?
quiz.hint: Look at where the BIG jump happens. The jump = from the last outer electron to the first inner electron.
quiz.explanation: 590→1145 (small jump) = removing outer electrons. 1145→4912 (BIG jump!) = all outer electrons gone. Two outer electrons = Group 2. The massive jump is because electrons in a lower shell are much harder to remove.

content.summary: When atoms absorb energy (heat or electricity), electrons jump to excited states. When they fall back down, they release energy as light (photons).
content.why_line_spectrum: Unlike white light (continuous), atoms produce LINE spectra. Why? Because electrons can ONLY exist at specific energy levels — quantum theory! They can only make specific jumps, releasing specific photon energies.
content.tip: Balmer series (n→2) is special because it produces VISIBLE light — red, blue-green, blue, violet. These are the lines you see in hydrogen's emission spectrum.
content.memory: Think of the energy levels like steps on a staircase. Electrons can only stand on steps, not between them. When they jump down, they release exactly the energy difference between those two steps.

quiz.question: Which series of hydrogen's emission spectrum corresponds to visible light?
quiz.hint: Remember: Lyman (UV), Balmer (Visible), Paschen (IR) — think of the electromagnetic spectrum from left to right.
quiz.explanation: Balmer series: electrons falling to n=2. The energy differences at this level correspond to visible wavelengths (400-700nm). Lyman is UV (higher energy), Paschen is IR (lower energy).

content.summary: To compare masses of atoms, we use relative scales — no units! Ar (relative atomic mass) compares a single atom to carbon-12. Mr (relative molecular mass) is the sum of Ar for all atoms in a molecule.
content.key_formula: Ar = mass of one atom / (mass of one carbon-12 atom / 12)
content.formula: Mr = sum of (Ar × number of atoms)
content.tip: Ar has NO units — it's a ratio. Think of it like a 'score' comparing atoms to carbon-12.
content.memory: ⚠️ Don't confuse Ar (one element) with Mr (whole molecule)!

quiz.question: What is the Mr of CO₂? (Ar: C=12, O=16)
quiz.explanation: Mr(CO₂) = 12 + 2(16) = 12 + 32 = 44. One carbon atom plus two oxygen atoms.

content.summary: The mole (mol) is a count — like a 'dozen' but astronomically larger. Avogadro's constant (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) tells us exactly how many particles are in one mole. Mass (m), molar mass (M), and moles (n) are linked by the most important formula in chemistry.
content.formula: n = m / M   (moles = mass / molar mass)
content.formula_example: n = 98g / 98 g mol⁻¹ = 1 mol of H₂SO₄
content.tip: M (molar mass) has the SAME numerical value as Mr, but units g mol⁻¹. M = Mr g/mol by definition!
content.memory: Molar mass M (g mol⁻¹) = Mr × 1 g/mol. So M and Mr have the same number but different units!

quiz.question: How many moles are in 36g of water? (Mr H₂O = 18)?
quiz.explanation: n = m/M = 36g / 18 g mol⁻¹ = 2 mol. Simple division — the key formula n = m/M is the most-used in ch03!

content.summary: Empirical formula = simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Molecular formula = actual number of atoms. To find empirical: convert % to moles → divide by smallest → round to whole numbers. Molecular = n × empirical, where n = Mr(molecular) / Mr(empirical).
content.formula: Empirical → divide each % by Ar → divide by smallest → whole numbers
content.molecular_example: Empirical CH₂O, Mr=60 → molecular = 2 × CH₂O = C₂H₄O₂
content.tip: If a question gives % composition by mass, start by assuming 100g total — then % becomes grams directly!
content.memory: Empirical = 'EGG-splest ratio' 📐. Molecular = actual number in one molecule. Start with % → moles → ratio → empirical.

quiz.question: A compound is 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: C=12, H=1, O=16)?
quiz.hint: Assume 100g: C=40g, H=6.7g, O=53.3g → divide by Ar → divide by smallest

content.summary: Gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules per unit volume. At RTP (25°C, 100 kPa): Vm = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹. At STP (0°C, 100 kPa): Vm = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹. The ideal gas equation handles any condition.
content.formula: pV = nRT  (pressure × volume = moles × R × temperature)
content.variables: p in Pa, V in m³, T in K, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, n in mol
content.molar_volumes: RTP: 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ (25°C, 100 kPa) | STP: 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ (0°C, 100 kPa)
content.tip: ⚠️ V in dm³ for molar volume: V (dm³) = n × 24. But convert to m³ for pV = nRT! 1 dm³ = 1×10⁻³ m³
content.memory: 24 at RTP, 22.7 at STP. 25°C=298K, 0°C=273K. Gas volume questions = n × Vm = m/M × Vm.

quiz.question: What volume does 2 mol of gas occupy at RTP? (Vm = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.explanation: V = 2 mol × 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 48.0 dm³. The molar volume × moles = gas volume!

content.summary: Concentration (c) = moles of solute per volume of solution. Molarity (M) in mol dm⁻³ = mol / dm³. Dilution formula: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ (moles stay the same). Titration: at equivalence, moles acid = stoichiometric ratio × moles base.
content.formula: c = n / V   (concentration = moles / volume in dm³)
content.dilution_example: 10 cm³ of 2 mol dm⁻³ HCl diluted to 100 cm³ → c₂ = 10×2/100 = 0.2 mol dm⁻³
content.tip: ⚠️ Always convert cm³ to dm³: divide by 1000! 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³. This trips up many students!
content.memory: c = n/V. Dilution: c drops when V increases (same moles in bigger container). Titration: look for equivalence point = equal moles ratio.

quiz.question: How many moles are in 250 cm³ of 0.5 mol dm⁻³ NaOH solution?
quiz.hint: n = c × V, but convert 250 cm³ to dm³ first

content.summary: Stoichiometry = using balanced equations to find amounts. Key steps: (1) Write balanced equation. (2) Convert given mass to moles (÷ M). (3) Use mole ratio from equation. (4) Convert back to mass (× M) or volume.
content.formula:
Balanced equation: aA + bB → cC
Mole ratio: nA : nB : nC = a : b : c
content.step_guide: 1. m → n (÷M). 2. Use ratio. 3. n → mass/volume (×M or ×24).
content.tip: Always check your mole ratio from the balanced equation's coefficients — NOT from eyeballing!
content.memory: The 'golden path': grams → moles → ratio → grams/mol/vol. Every stoichiometry question follows this route!

quiz.question: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many moles of H₂O from 4 mol H₂?
quiz.explanation: From the equation: 2 mol H₂ produces 2 mol H₂O. Ratio is 1:1, so 4 mol H₂ → 4 mol H₂O.

content.summary: Limiting reagent = reactant that runs out first, stopping the reaction. Find it by dividing moles of each reactant by its coefficient — the smallest result is limiting. % yield measures efficiency. Atom economy measures 'greenness' — how much product contains desired atoms.
content.limiting_method: 1. Calculate moles of each reactant. 2. Divide by stoichiometric coefficient. 3. Smallest value = limiting reagent.
content.atom_economy: Atom economy = (Mr of desired product / total Mr of all products) × 100%
content.atom_economy_example: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: Mr(NH₃)=17, total products=34 → economy = 2×17/34×100 = 100% (all atoms in product)
content.tip: Theoretical yield is calculated from the LIMITING REAGENT — never from the excess!
content.memory: Limiting = 'the one that runs out first' — divide moles by coefficient. Yield = actual/theoretical. Atom economy = 'green' measure of how much ends up in product.

quiz.question: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. If 1 mol N₂ and 3 mol H₂ react in exact ratio, and 0.8 mol NH₃ is obtained, what is the % yield?
quiz.explanation: Exact 1:3 ratio → neither limiting. Theoretical = 2 mol NH₃. % yield = (0.8/2)×100 = 40%. Actual < theoretical is normal: side reactions, incomplete conversion, product loss during handling.

content.summary: 2 bp: linear (180°). 3 bp: trigonal planar (120°). 4 bp: tetrahedral (109.5°). 3 bp + 1 lp: pyramidal (~107°). 2 bp + 2 lp: bent/V-shaped (~104.5°). 5 bp: trigonal bipyramidal. 6 bp: octahedral (90°).

levels.title: Effect of lone pairs on bond angles

content.summary: Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, reducing bond angles. Each lone pair reduces angles by ~2.5°.
content.tip: Order of repulsion: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp.

content.summary: sp³: tetrahedral (methane, water, ammonia). sp²: trigonal planar, one unhybridised p orbital for π bond (ethene, BF₃). sp: linear, two unhybridised p orbitals for two π bonds (ethyne, CO₂, BeCl₂).
content.key_formula:
sp³ hybridisation → tetrahedral (109.5°)
sp² → trigonal planar, 1 unhybridised p for π bond
sp → linear, 2 unhybridised p for 2 π bonds

content.summary: If ΔEN > 1.7: ionic. If 0.4 < ΔEN < 1.7: polar covalent.
content.key_formula:
ΔEN > 1.7 → ionic
0.4 < ΔEN < 1.7 → polar covalent
ΔEN < 0.4 → non-polar covalent
content.tip: If ΔEN < 0.4: non-polar covalent. Pauling values: F(4.0) > O(3.5) > N(3.0) > Cl(3.0) > Br(2.8) > C(2.5) > H(2.1).

content.summary: Hydrogen bonds (~20 kJ/mol) > Permanent dipole-dipole (~2-5 kJ/mol) > Van der Waals/London (depends on size).
content.tip: VdW increases with Mr (more electrons = larger temporary dipoles).

content.summary: Must have: H bonded directly to N, O, or F in one molecule AND a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule.
content.tip: Examples: H₂O (2 H-bonds per molecule), NH₃, HF, DNA base pairs.

content.summary: High melting/boiling points (strong ionic bonds). Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (mobile ions).
content.tip: Hard but brittle. Soluble in polar solvents.

content.summary: Diamond: 4 C-C bonds, tetrahedral, very hard, no electrical conduction. Graphite: 3 C-C bonds, layers, delocalized π electrons (conducts), lubricant.
content.key_formula: Sigma & Pi bonds: Single bond = 1 σ, Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π, Triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π
content.tip: SiO₂: giant lattice, very hard, high mp.

content.summary: Single bond = 1 σ bond. Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π bond.
content.tip: Triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π bonds. Rotation is possible around σ bonds but NOT around π bonds (restricted rotation in C=C causes geometric isomerism).

content.summary: Positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. High electrical/thermal conductivity (mobile electrons).
content.tip: Malleable/ductile (layers slide). High melting point (strong attraction). Increases with more delocalised electrons and smaller ion radius.

content.summary: Molecules are point masses with negligible volume. No intermolecular forces.
content.tip: Collisions are perfectly elastic. Average KE ∝ absolute temperature (T in Kelvin). Molecules move in random directions.

content.summary: At high pressure: real gas volume > ideal (repulsive forces) or < ideal (attractive forces dominate). At low temperature: attractive forces significant → real gas volume < ideal.
content.tip: Ideal behaviour: high T, low P.

content.summary: Ionic (NaCl): high mp, conducts when molten/dissolved. Giant covalent (SiO₂, diamond): very high mp, no conduction.
content.tip: Simple molecular (ice, I₂): low mp, no conduction. Metallic (Fe, Cu): high mp, conducts.

content.summary: Diamond: sp³, tetrahedral, hardest natural substance, insulator. Graphite: sp², layered, conductor (delocalised electrons), lubricant.
content.tip: Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀): spherical, molecular, used in nanotechnology.

levels.title: Effect of structure on melting point

content.summary: Giant structures (ionic, covalent, metallic) have high melting points (must break many bonds). Simple molecular structures have low melting points (only overcome weak Van der Waals).
content.tip: Larger molecules have higher melting points (more VdW).

content.summary: Temperature: 298 K (25°C). Pressure: 100 kPa (1 bar).
content.key_formula: Standard conditions: T = 298 K, P = 100 kPa, [soln] = 1 mol dm⁻³
content.tip: Concentration: 1 mol dm⁻³ for solutions. All substances in their standard states.

content.summary: ΔHreaction = ΣΔHf°(products) − ΣΔHf°(reactants). OR use a two-step Hess cycle: route 1 (direct) = route 2 (via intermediates).
content.tip: ΔHf° of elements in standard states = 0.

content.summary: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Bonds broken: endothermic (+).
content.tip: Bonds formed: exothermic (−). Mean bond enthalpies give approximate values; exact values require specific compound data.

content.summary: q = mcΔT (m = mass of solution in g, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water, ΔT = temperature change). ΔH = −q/n (negative sign: exothermic when T rises).
content.key_formula: q = mcΔT (m = mass/g, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔT = temp change)
content.tip: Limitations: heat loss to surroundings, incomplete reaction.

content.summary: Exothermic: products lower than reactants, ΔH < 0. Endothermic: products higher than reactants, ΔH > 0.
content.tip: Activation energy (Ea) is always positive. Catalyst lowers Ea but does NOT change ΔH.

content.summary: ΔHf°: forming 1 mol compound from elements in standard states. ΔHc°: completely burning 1 mol substance.
content.tip: ΔHat°(element): forming 1 mol gaseous atoms from element. ΔHat°(compound): forming gaseous atoms from 1 mol compound.

content.summary: 1. Free element = 0. 2.
content.key_formula: Oxidation Number Rules: Free element = 0, O = −2, H = +1, Sum = charge
content.tip: Monatomic ion = ionic charge. 3. O = −2 (except in peroxides −1, OF₂ +2). 4. H = +1 (except metal hydrides −1). 5. Sum = overall charge of species.

content.summary: 1. Balance atoms other than O and H. 2.
content.tip: Balance O by adding H₂O. 3. Balance H by adding H⁺. 4. Balance charge by adding e⁻. 5. Combine half-equations (multiply to equalise electrons). Acidic conditions: use H⁺/H₂O. Alkaline: use OH⁻/H₂O.

content.summary: The species that gains electrons (is reduced) is the oxidising agent. The species that loses electrons (is oxidised) is the reducing agent.
content.tip: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

content.summary: MnO₄⁻ (KMnO₄): Mn +7 → +2 (acidic) or +4. Cr₂O₇²⁻: Cr +6 → +3.
content.tip: H₂O₂: O −1 → −2. Cl₂: Cl 0 → −1. O₂: O 0 → −2. Fe³⁺: Fe +3 → +2.

content.summary: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺. SO₂/SO₃²⁻ → SO₄²⁻.
content.tip: I⁻ → I₂. H₂O₂ → O₂ (also oxidising agent). Metals (e.g. Fe, Zn) → metal ions.

content.summary: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO (Cl: 0 → −1 and +1). H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂ (O: −1 → −2 and 0).
content.tip: Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺.

content.summary: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = [C]^c × [D]^d / ([A]^a × [B]^b). Pure solids and liquids are NOT included (activity = 1).
content.tip: Units depend on Δn = (c+d) − (a+b).

content.summary: Kp = Π p(products) / Π p(reactants). Partial pressure p = mole fraction × total pressure.
content.key_formula:
Kp = Π p(products) / Π p(reactants)
Partial pressure p = mole fraction × P_total
content.tip: Mole fraction = n(gas) / n(total gas). Kp units: Pa raised to Δn.

levels.title: Effect of changes on equilibrium (Le Chatelier)

content.summary: Increase concentration of reactant → shift right (more products). Increase pressure (gas) → shift to side with fewer moles of gas.
content.tip: Increase temperature → shift in endothermic direction. Catalyst → no effect on position, only reaches equilibrium faster.

content.summary: Increasing T shifts equilibrium endothermic direction. If forward reaction is exothermic: Kc decreases with increasing T.
content.key_formula:
Exothermic: Kc ↓ as T ↑
Endothermic: Kc ↑ as T ↑
content.tip: If forward reaction is endothermic: Kc increases with increasing T. Catalyst does NOT affect Kc.

content.summary: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. High pressure → higher yield (fewer moles gas on right).
content.key_formula:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹
Compromise: 450°C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst
content.tip: Low temperature → higher yield (exothermic). But low T is slow → compromise: 450°C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst.

content.summary: Compromise conditions balance yield and rate. Very high P is expensive (engineering costs).
content.tip: Catalyst increases rate without affecting yield. Economic viability requires continuous process with recycling of unreacted gases.
